slow_query_postmeta.title: Slow postmeta query
slow_query_postmeta.body: This query scans or joins wp_postmeta, which grows with every product/post and has no useful index for this access pattern. This is the exact query shape Scalability Pro fixes with covering indexes and query rewrites.

slow_query_found_rows.title: SQL_CALC_FOUND_ROWS
slow_query_found_rows.body: SQL_CALC_FOUND_ROWS forces MySQL to count every matching row just to show pagination totals. Scalability Pro removes it from key queries.

slow_query_rand.title: ORDER BY rand()
slow_query_rand.body: ORDER BY rand() forces a full table scan and sort on every page view and gets slower as your content grows. The component running it should pick random items a cheaper way (e.g. random offset).

slow_query_like.title: Leading-wildcard LIKE
slow_query_like.body: LIKE '%term%' cannot use an index and scans the whole table. If this powers your search, a dedicated search plugin such as Super Speedy Search replaces it with indexed lookups.

slow_query_tax.title: Nested taxonomy query
slow_query_tax.body: Deeply nested term_relationships joins slow down as your catalogue grows. Scalability Pro's taxonomy query optimisation and Super Speedy Filters both target this pattern.

slow_query_generic.title: Slow query
slow_query_generic.body: This query exceeds the slow threshold. Check whether the component really needs it on every page load, and whether an index would help.

big_result_set.title: Large result set
big_result_set.body: Queries returning hundreds of rows are the usual cause of high RAM per page view: every row is hydrated into PHP memory. If this component regularly fetches this much data, it is a prime suspect for Plugin Impact Analysis.

query_loop.title: Queries in a loop
query_loop.body: The measured query count is high. Inspect the initiating caller and attribution chain for an N+1 loop, then confirm whether batching or caching is appropriate.

dupe_queries.title: Duplicate queries
dupe_queries.body: The same query ran repeatedly in one page load. Inspect the initiating caller to determine whether request-local caching, batching or another change is appropriate.

slow_http.title: Blocking HTTP call during page load
slow_http.body: This component makes a blocking HTTP request while your page renders - every visitor waits for a remote server (licence checks and geo lookups are common offenders). These calls belong in cron, not page loads.

autoload_bloat.title: Autoloaded options bloat
autoload_bloat.body: Your autoloaded options exceed 1MB and are loaded on every request into memory. Find the biggest autoloaded rows and set autoload=no or delete leftovers from removed plugins.

no_object_cache.title: No persistent object cache
no_object_cache.body: This site has a large database but no persistent object cache (Redis/Memcached). Every request recomputes work that could be cached in memory. Ask your host to enable Redis and install a drop-in.

old_php.title: Outdated PHP
old_php.body: PHP 8+ is significantly faster than PHP 7.x for WordPress workloads. Upgrading PHP is usually the cheapest speed win available.

duplicate_functionality.title: Overlapping plugins
duplicate_functionality.body: These active plugins are in the same broad capability category. Their configuration was not inspected, so review which modules are enabled before deciding whether any functionality overlaps.

potential_overlap_review.title: Review potentially overlapping configuration
potential_overlap_review.body: These active plugins are in the same broad capability category, but activation alone does not prove that the same modules are enabled. Review their settings; do not remove a plugin based on this finding alone.

blocking_mail.title: Slow email construction
blocking_mail.body: Building this email blocked the request for a long time - heavyweight templates or an SMTP plugin doing expensive setup on every send. Order status changes and checkouts wait on this.

cache_blind.title: Ignores the object cache
cache_blind.body: This component ran essentially the same queries with the object cache on and off - it caches nothing, so your Redis/Memcached investment does nothing for it. Prime candidate for replacement or a caching layer.

cache_friendly.title: Uses the object cache well
cache_friendly.body: This component's query count drops sharply when the object cache is available - it is written cache-aware. Keep it.

security_block.title: Profiling requests blocked
security_block.body: A security layer blocked this plugin's self-profiling requests, so some pages could not be measured. Whitelist your own server's IP in the named security plugin and re-run the analysis.

cache_safety_review.title: Review visitor-specific content
cache_safety_review.body: This is a passive safety scan, not proof that content leaks or that a named component caused it. Review the hazards and candidate components, then compare controlled guest, customer and basket responses before enabling shared caching for those states.

unindexed_query.title: Query with no usable index
unindexed_query.body: MySQL cannot use an index for this query, so it reads every row in the table and throws away the ones that do not match. It may be fast today because the table is small - it gets linearly slower as your content grows, and it is one of the most common causes of a site that was fine last year. Fixes, in order of preference: get the plugin author to add the missing index, add a covering index yourself, or change the query shape.

over_examining_query.title: Query reads far more rows than it returns
over_examining_query.body: MySQL read a very large number of rows to produce a small answer. That is wasted disk and CPU on every single request, and it is the shape that turns a fast site slow as your content grows. It usually means a missing or unusable index, a join in the wrong order, or a filter MySQL cannot push down into the index. This figure is what the database actually did, not an estimate.

checkout_slow_step.title: A checkout step is making your customer wait
checkout_slow_step.body: This step of the purchase took longer than it should on the server alone, before any browser work. Expand the step to see which component dominated it, then decide whether that work has to happen while the customer is waiting or can be deferred to a background job. Time spent before the payment is taken is the expensive kind: the customer can still abandon during it.

order_management_slow_step.title: An order-management step is slowing your staff down
order_management_slow_step.body: This wp-admin step took longer than it should on the server alone. It happens after the purchase, so it does not delay the customer or risk the sale, but your staff pays the cost on every order they handle. Expand the step to see the component, queries, outbound calls, mail and sampled functions responsible, then decide what can be cached, removed or deferred.

checkout_component_cost.title: One plugin owns a large share of your checkout
checkout_component_cost.body: This component accounted for a large share of the server time across the whole purchase. That is attribution from measured stack samples, not an isolation experiment - the decisive test is re-running the checkout flow with the plugin briefly deactivated on a staging copy. Per-plugin checkout isolation is planned for Plugin Impact Analysis.

checkout_blocking_http.title: Your checkout waits on an outside server
checkout_blocking_http.body: Blocking outbound HTTP calls ran while the customer waited. Tax services, fraud screening, address validation, CRM and accounting syncs are the usual culprits - and so are cache-purge plugins that fetch your own site's pages inline: every order status change can set off another round of purges, each one a full page request your customer waits for. If the host shown is your own domain, look at your cache plugin's purge settings first. Otherwise ask the plugin's author whether the call can be deferred to a background job or cached.

checkout_mail_inline.title: Order emails are sent inside the checkout request
checkout_mail_inline.body: Your customer is waiting for your mail server. WooCommerce can hand transactional emails to a background queue instead: enable the deferred transactional emails feature (WooCommerce > Settings > Advanced > Features), or use an SMTP plugin that queues rather than sends inline. This is usually one of the easiest seconds to remove from a checkout.

checkout_dupe_queries.title: A checkout step repeats the same query
checkout_dupe_queries.body: Byte-identical queries ran several times inside one step, so the same rows were fetched more than once. That is normally a missing cache or a lookup inside a loop in the component named. On checkout it is worth fixing even when each query is fast, because it happens at the moment the customer is most likely to leave.

order_management_dupe_queries.title: An order-management step repeats the same query
order_management_dupe_queries.body: Byte-identical queries ran several times while an administrator handled the order, so the same rows were fetched more than once. That is normally a missing cache or a lookup inside a loop in the component named. It does not delay checkout, but it adds avoidable staff time to every order handled.

checkout_purge_order_pages.title: Your cache plugin purges the order itself on every checkout
checkout_purge_order_pages.body: A cache-purge plugin treated the new order as a page and fetched its permalink to purge it. Orders are not public pages: with WooCommerce's High-Performance Order Storage that URL is a placeholder draft at /?p=<order id>, so each purge is a slow request to a page that does not exist, often running to the HTTP timeout - and it fires again on every order note and status change. The placeholder post cannot be removed; it is how HPOS stays compatible with older code. The fix is to stop the purge plugin reacting to order post types: with nginx-helper the trigger is its comment hook (order notes are comments), which can be unhooked for order notes, or every such request short-circuited via pre_http_request. Scalability Pro's checkout purge shield does this automatically.

checkout_amp_purge_missing.title: Your cache plugin purges AMP pages this site does not have
checkout_amp_purge_missing.body: The purge plugin fetches the /amp/ variant of each purged URL as a plain request, and with no AMP plugin installed every one of those renders a full 404 page while your customer waits. In nginx-helper this is the Purge AMP URL setting - turn it off, or let Scalability Pro's checkout purge shield drop these requests. If you later add AMP, turn it back on.

checkout_self_fetch_failed.title: Your site calls itself during checkout and the call fails
checkout_self_fetch_failed.body: A blocking request from this site to its own URL ran until it failed or timed out, while the customer waited, and the response was never usable. This is almost always a cache purge or preload gone wrong - the caller is shown on the outbound call. Fix the calling plugin's configuration or defer the call; a failing self-request is pure wasted checkout time.

autoload_coverage.title: Autoload settings do not match what your pages actually read
autoload_coverage.body: This analysis recorded every option each profiled page read. The rows below were never read on any page in this run, or are read on nearly every page but are not autoloaded. Autoload is only a caching decision, so changing it cannot break your site - a wrong choice costs speed, not correctness. Review the SQL before running it, and remember this scan cannot see cron jobs, webhooks or admin-ajax.

isolation_reaction.title: A plugin reacted to another being excluded
isolation_reaction.body: While this plugin's dependency was excluded from a test request, it tried to switch a plugin on or off, or to run a destructive database statement. Nothing was allowed to happen: your plugin list, its routines and your database were untouched, and the pair will be measured together from now on. Run the analysis again for a trustworthy verdict on the pair.

price_affecting.source: Super Speedy Ajax Prices ssap_known_price_plugin_patterns(), copied 21 October 2026

quotes.text: Dave sets up full-page caching so eligible shop and content pages come from cache for anonymous visitors, logged-in customers and shoppers with a basket. Each visitor still sees their own prices, stock and basket.

figures.text: On Dave’s own store, a shopper with an item in their basket got cached pages with an 80 ms median time to first byte (3 requests, measured 13 August 2026). All three were verified cache HITs. That’s Dave’s own site measured from Athens. A cached page’s time to first byte depends mainly on the speed of the cache service and where the visitor’s computer is, so Dave measures your store before and after rather than quoting you his.

supported_systems.text: Supported systems include WP Rocket, W3 Total Cache, LiteSpeed Cache, Nginx FastCGI cache, Varnish, Cloudflare APO and Cloudflare Cache Rules.

quotes.text: Cache WooCommerce shop, category and product pages without serving the wrong personalised price. Super Speedy Ajax Prices replaces prices, stock and Add to Cart state for each visitor in one batched request after the cached page loads.

cache_education.text: Most WordPress caching tools bypass a page as soon as they see a logged-in cookie or an active basket. That protects correctness, but it also leaves some of the store’s most valuable visitors waiting for PHP, WordPress and WooCommerce on every page view.
Eligible home, shop, product category, product, article and other shared pages. Logging in or adding an item to the basket does not make those pages uncached.
Eligible catalogue and content pages can remain fully cached while each visitor’s prices, stock and basket state are loaded through a per-visitor AJAX request.

This implementation uses cross-user caching. Every visitor can receive the same safe, non-personal cached HTML while their own prices, country or tax prices, stock, basket state, account indicator and other agreed personal regions are loaded separately.
The separate Cart/Basket, Checkout, My Account and any other page that shows private information stay outside the shared cache.
Every WooCommerce store has a different personalisation surface, and getting it wrong can expose one visitor’s information to another.

The plugin itself is built for ordinary visitors: your caching plugin serves guests from cache, while visitors with a basket or a login bypass the cache as normal and see live pages. Serving fully cached pages to basket holders and even logged-in customers is possible as well, but most themes and plugin stacks need compatibility work first.
Page caching and object caching solve different problems, so object caching is not used as a substitute for full-page cache.
A TTFB number only means something on a confirmed cache HIT.
